title: Which parameter fits best?
objectives: Write a likelihood and read it as a function of the parameter.
Compare two parameter values by their likelihood ratio.

screens.title: Which coin made this?
screens.prose: A coin with unknown chance of heads $p$ is flipped three times: H, H, T. For any $p$, the chance of exactly this sequence is $p \cdot p \cdot (1 - p)$. The curve plots that chance against $p$.

derive.caption: At $p$ = {{fixed(p, 2)}} the chance of H, H, T is {{fixed(p*p*(1-p), 4)}}

screens.question: Slide $p$ to the value that makes H, H, T most likely.

hints.text: Watch the number in the caption. Where does it stop rising?
The highest point of the curve is between 0.6 and 0.7.
Slide slowly from 0.6 to 0.7. The caption peaks at 0.1481, near 0.67.

feedback.correct: The chance of H, H, T is largest near $p = 0.67$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the caption stops rising and starts to fall.

byKey.fair: You stopped near a fair coin. Keep sliding right: the caption still rises after 0.5.
byKey.top: A coin near $p = 1$ almost never gives the T. The caption falls towards 0 there.

explain.text: You stopped at the top of the curve, $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$. There the chance of H, H, T is $\tfrac{4}{27} \approx 0.148$, more than at any other $p$. Two heads in three flips is best explained by a coin that shows heads two thirds of the time.

screens.prose: Now change the data. The control $k$ sets how many of the three flips were heads, and the curve becomes $p^k (1 - p)^{3 - k}$. Try each $k$, and slide $p$ along the curve.

derive.caption: {{k}} heads in 3: at $p$ = {{fixed(p, 2)}} the chance is {{fixed(pow(p, k)*pow(1-p, 3-k), 4)}}

screens.question: Set $k = 3$, so all three flips were heads. Where is the curve highest?

options.text: At $p = 1$, the right-hand end
At $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$, as before
options.why: You kept the peak from H, H, T. With $k = 3$ the curve is $p^3$, which rises all the way to $p = 1$.

options.text: At $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$
options.why: You assumed the coin is fair. With three heads and no tails, a fair coin explains the data less well than a two-headed one.

options.text: Nowhere: the curve has no peak
options.why: The curve has no flat top, but it still has a highest point. It is at the end of the range, $p = 1$.

feedback.correct: All heads is explained best by a coin that always lands heads.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $k = 3$ and slide $p$ to both ends.

explain.text: With $k = 3$ the curve is $p^3$, which keeps rising until $p = 1$. A coin that always shows heads gives H, H, H with chance 1. The best $p$ can sit at the very end of its range.

screens.title: The likelihood
screens.prose: The curve you slid along has a name. With the data fixed at H, H, T, the **likelihood** is $L(p) = P(\text{H, H, T} \mid p) = p^2(1 - p)$. It is the chance of the data, read as a function of the parameter $p$.
screens.question: A fair coin has $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$. What is $L(\tfrac{1}{2})$, the chance of exactly H, H, T?

hints.text: Each flip has its own factor. What are the three factors at $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$?
The curve crosses the line $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ just above 0.12.
Multiply $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply one factor per flip: $p$ for each head and $1 - p$ for the tail.

byKey.orders: You counted all three orders of two heads and a tail. The data is the one sequence H, H, T.
byKey.heads-only: You multiplied the two heads and left out the tail. The T contributes a factor $1 - p$ too.
byKey.just-p: That is the chance of one head. The data is three flips, so three factors multiply.

explain.text: You multiplied one factor per flip: $\tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{8}$. Counting all three orders would multiply every $L(p)$ by 3, which moves no peak. Either version is a valid likelihood.

screens.prose: To compare two values of $p$, divide their likelihoods. The **likelihood ratio** says how many times better one explains the data than the other.
screens.question: What is $L(\tfrac{2}{3}) / L(\tfrac{1}{2})$? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: You already have $L(\tfrac{1}{2})$. Work out $L(\tfrac{2}{3}) = (\tfrac{2}{3})^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{3}$.
Divide: $\tfrac{4}{27} \div \tfrac{1}{8} = \tfrac{32}{27}$.

feedback.correct: The data is about 1.19 times as likely under $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

byKey.inverted: You divided the other way round. Put $L(\tfrac{2}{3})$ on top.
byKey.difference: You subtracted the likelihoods. A ratio compares them by division, so the scale of $L$ drops out.

explain.text: You divided $\tfrac{4}{27}$ by $\tfrac{1}{8}$ to get $\tfrac{32}{27} \approx 1.19$. The best $p$ beats a fair coin, but only by 19%. Three flips cannot tell these two coins apart with any confidence.

screens.prose: Same data, H, H, T. Two other candidates: $p = 0.45$ and $p = 0.85$. The second is closer to the peak at $\tfrac{2}{3}$.
screens.question: Which value explains H, H, T better?

options.text: $p = 0.85$, because it is closer to the peak
options.why: You judged by distance from the peak. The curve falls faster on the right, so $L(0.85) = 0.108$ is below $L(0.45) = 0.111$.

options.text: Neither: they are about equally far from the peak
options.why: You assumed the curve is symmetric about its peak. It is not: it drops steeply towards $p = 1$.

options.text: $p = 0.85$, because the data is mostly heads
options.why: Mostly heads favours $p$ above $\tfrac{1}{2}$, but $0.85$ makes the tail too unlikely. Compute both likelihoods.

hints.text: Compute $L(0.45)$ and $L(0.85)$ from $p^2(1 - p)$.
Compare where each dashed line meets the curve.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $p^2(1 - p)$ at both values and compare.

explain.text: You compared $L(0.45) = 0.111$ with $L(0.85) = 0.108$, a ratio of 1.03. The likelihood is not symmetric about its peak. Only the heights matter, not the distances.

screens.prose: Ana reads the curve and says: “$L(\tfrac{2}{3}) = 0.148$, so there is a 14.8% chance that this coin has $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$.” The shaded area is everything under the curve.
screens.question: What is wrong with Ana's statement?

options.text: 0.148 is the chance of the data if $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$, not a chance about $p$
Nothing: $L(p)$ is the chance of $p$ given the data
options.why: You read $L(p)$ as $P(p \mid \text{data})$. The area under the curve is $\tfrac{1}{12}$, not 1, so these heights are not chances for $p$.

options.text: She should multiply by 3 for the orders: a 44.4% chance
options.why: Multiplying by 3 changes the chance of the data, not of $p$. The statement still runs the wrong way round.

options.text: 0.148 is the chance that the next flip is heads
options.why: If $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$, the next flip is heads with chance $\tfrac{2}{3}$. The likelihood is about the flips already seen.

hints.text: Which way round is the condition in $P(\text{H, H, T} \mid p)$?
Look at the shaded area. A distribution over $p$ would have area 1.
$L(p)$ fixes $p$ and asks about the data. A chance about $p$ would need a starting belief about $p$.

feedback.correct: The likelihood is the chance of the data, for each fixed $p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what $L(p)$ conditions on.

byKey.posterior: You read $L(p)$ as $P(p \mid \text{data})$. The area under the curve is $\tfrac{1}{12}$, not 1, so these heights are not chances for $p$.

explain.text: $L(\tfrac{2}{3})$ is $P(\text{data} \mid p = \tfrac{2}{3})$, with the condition on $p$. Its area is $\tfrac{1}{12}$, so it is not a distribution over $p$. Turning it into $P(p \mid \text{data})$ needs a prior belief about $p$, which we meet in level 3.

screens.prose:
Every time, you multiplied one factor per observation. For data $x_1, \dots, x_n$, independent given the parameter $\theta$:

$$L(\theta) = P(\text{data} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i \mid \theta)$$

The data stays fixed and $\theta$ moves. Compare two values of $\theta$ by the ratio $L(\theta_1) / L(\theta_2)$.
screens.question: Five flips: H, T, T, H, T. Which is the likelihood $L(p)$?

options.why: You gave the heads the tails' count. There are two heads, so $p$ appears twice.
You added the factors. Independent flips multiply, one factor each.

options.text: $\big(p(1 - p)\big)^5$
options.why: That gives every flip both factors. Each flip is either a head ($p$) or a tail ($1 - p$), not both.

feedback.correct: Two factors of $p$ and three of $1 - p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write one factor per flip and multiply them.

explain.text: Each head gives a factor $p$ and each tail $1 - p$, and independence multiplies them. The order does not matter, so H, T, T, H, T gives $p^2(1 - p)^3$.

screens.prose: Write the likelihood yourself. A coin with chance of heads $p$ is flipped four times, independently, and gives H, T, H, H.
screens.question: Enter $L(p)$, the chance of this sequence.

hints.text: Write one factor per flip, in order.
H gives $p$ and T gives $1 - p$.
$p \cdot (1 - p) \cdot p \cdot p = p^3(1 - p)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Three heads and one tail: multiply one factor for each.

byKey.swap: You swapped the counts. There are three heads, so $p$ appears three times.
byKey.add: You added the factors. The flips are independent, so their chances multiply.
byKey.orders: You counted the 4 orders of three heads and a tail. The data is this one sequence, so leave out the 4.

explain.text: Each head contributes $p$ and the tail $1 - p$: $L(p) = p^3(1 - p)$. Sliding along this curve would put the peak at $p = \tfrac{3}{4}$.

screens.title: A strategy's hit rate
screens.prose: A strategy's backtest shows 12 winning trades out of 20. Treat each trade as winning with chance $h$, independently. The curve is the likelihood of that exact record, $L(h) = h^{12}(1 - h)^{8}$, drawn in millionths.
screens.question: Slide $h$ to the hit rate that best explains the record.

hints.text: Watch the caption. Where does it stop rising?
The peak is between 0.55 and 0.65.
Slide to 0.60. The caption reads about 1.427 millionths, its largest value.

feedback.correct: The record is most likely when $h = 0.6$, its win share.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the caption is as large as it gets.

byKey.fair: You stopped near a coin-flip strategy. The caption still rises past 0.5.

explain.text: The peak is at $h = 0.6$, the share of winning trades. But $L(0.5) / L(0.6) = 0.67$, so a coin-flip strategy explains the record two thirds as well. Twenty trades are weak evidence of skill.

screens.title: Calm or volatile?
screens.prose: A stock's returns for one week are in the table, in %. Model each day as normal with mean 0 and sd $\sigma$, independently. The table gives each day's density under $\sigma = 1\%$ and under $\sigma = 2\%$.
screens.question: What is the likelihood ratio $L(\sigma = 1\%) / L(\sigma = 2\%)$ for the week?

widget.label: Likelihood ratio
widget.accept: any value within 2% of 5.55. Exactly $2^5 e^{-0.375 \times 4.67} \approx 5.554$.

hints.text: Each $L$ is the product of its column, because the days are independent.
It is quicker to divide day by day: day 1 gives $0.1942 / 0.1666 = 1.166$.
The five daily ratios are 1.166, 1.573, 1.821, 0.860 and 1.934. Multiply them.

feedback.correct: The calm model explains the week about 5.6 times better.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each column, then divide the two products.

byKey.inverted: You divided the 2% likelihood by the 1% one. Put $\sigma = 1\%$ on top.
byKey.added: You added the densities. Independent days multiply, so take the product of each column.

explain.text: You multiplied five daily densities in each column and divided: $0.000978 / 0.000176 \approx 5.55$. Only day 4, the 1.5% fall, favoured the volatile model. Small moves are much more likely under the calm one.

ideas: The likelihood $L(\theta)$ is the chance of the data you saw, read as a function of the parameter.
Its peak is the parameter value that best explains the data, and it can sit at the end of the range.
Compare two parameter values by the ratio of their likelihoods. $L$ is not a distribution over $\theta$.

formula.name: Likelihood of independent data
formula.note: The data is fixed; $\theta$ moves. Its area need not be 1.

summary.trap: $L(\tfrac{2}{3}) = 0.148$ is the chance of the data when $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$, not the chance that $p = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

quiz.prose: A coin gives H, H, H, T.
quiz.question: What is $L(0.75) / L(0.5)$? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $p^3(1 - p)$ at both values, then divide.

byKey.inverted: You divided the other way round. Put $L(0.75)$ on top.

quiz.prose: A coin is flipped five times and lands tails every time.
quiz.question: Which value of $p$, the chance of heads, makes this data most likely?

options.why: You kept some chance of heads in reserve. $L(p) = (1 - p)^5$ is largest when $1 - p$ is largest, at $p = 0$.
You assumed the coin is fair. A fair coin gives five tails with chance only $\tfrac{1}{32}$.

options.text: No value: there are no heads to estimate from
options.why: $L(p) = (1 - p)^5$ still has a highest point. It sits at the end of the range.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $L(p)$ and see where it is largest.

explain.text: Five tails give $L(p) = (1 - p)^5$, which falls as $p$ rises. Its highest point is the end of the range, $p = 0$, where $L = 1$.

quiz.prose: For the flips H, H, T, the likelihood is $L(p) = p^2(1 - p)$.
quiz.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: $L(0.6)$ is the chance of H, H, T when $p = 0.6$
$L(0.6)$ is the chance that $p = 0.6$, given H, H, T
options.why: That reads the condition the wrong way round. Chances about $p$ need a prior.

options.text: The area under $L(p)$ from 0 to 1 must be 1
options.why: That holds for a density over $p$. The area under this $L$ is $\tfrac{1}{12}$.

options.text: $L(p) + L(1 - p) = 1$ for every $p$

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $L(p) = P(\text{data} \mid p)$: ask what is fixed.

explain.text: $L(p)$ fixes $p$ and gives the chance of the data. It is not a distribution over $p$; its area here is $\tfrac{1}{12}$.

quiz.prose: A trader wins 6 trades and loses 4. Compare a win chance of 0.55 with one of 0.45.
quiz.question: What is $L(0.55) / L(0.45)$? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each likelihood as $h^6(1 - h)^4$ and divide.

byKey.inverted: You divided the other way round. Put $L(0.55)$ on top.
byKey.wins-only: You compared the wins and left out the losses. Each loss contributes $1 - h$.

explain.text: The ratio is $\left(\tfrac{0.55}{0.45}\right)^6 \left(\tfrac{0.45}{0.55}\right)^4 = \left(\tfrac{11}{9}\right)^2 \approx 1.49$. Four of the six wins cancel against the four losses.
